title: Multi-Armed Bandits with Minimum Revenue Constraints
one_liner: When you must decide which arm to pull in each context while keeping every arm above a minimum reward, this paper trades off between chasing high rewards and obeying the fairness rule.
lead: Imagine a recommendation system that must show ads fairly: each advertiser needs a minimum number of views across all users. But you also want to maximize clicks. This is a bandit problem where you learn which arm is best in each context, but you cannot just greedily chase the highest reward—you must also keep each arm above its threshold. This paper designs two algorithms that sit at opposite ends of a tradeoff: one chases reward and breaks the fairness rule sometimes, the other obeys fairness strictly but leaves rewards on the table.

paras: A bandit problem is a choice machine: in each round, you pick one of several options (arms) without knowing their rewards in advance, get feedback, and repeat. A multi-armed bandit learns which arm is best over time. But real systems add constraints: if you are allocating views across advertisers, each one needs a minimum. If you are routing traffic across servers, each must handle a fair load. If you are doing clinical trials, each treatment must accumulate enough data. Greedily pulling the highest-reward arm ignores these fairness rules.

A beginner might try this: play each arm just enough to hit its minimum, then chase the highest-reward arm forever. This fails because the highest-reward arm changes depending on context—who is using the system, what time it is, what their preferences are. In some contexts, a low-reward arm must be played to keep it above its minimum, eating into reward. The trade-off between reward and fairness is real and unavoidable.

callout.html: The paper designs two algorithms that navigate a Pareto frontier: one prioritizes reward and sometimes breaks fairness, the other prioritizes fairness and sometimes sacrifices reward.

panels.title: 1. Two arms, two contexts

panels.title: 2. Without fairness rules
panels.caption: Greedy: always chase the locally best arm. Red gets 95% of plays, Blue starves.

panels.title: 3. With minimum constraints
panels.viz_args: Red needs 40%, Blue needs 40%, Slack left 20%
panels.caption: Each arm must hit a minimum across all contexts. Now we have room to optimize.

panels.title: 4. Optimistic algorithm (OLP)
panels.caption: Assumes best-case rewards to pursue high performance. Learns fast but may violate constraints.

panels.title: 5. Pessimistic algorithm (OPLP)
panels.caption: Assumes worst-case to stay safe. Respects constraints but leaves some reward unclaimed.

paras: The paper changes the allocation rule—the mixture of plays across arms in each context. Instead of a fixed greedy rule or a naive uniform split, the algorithm re-solves a linear program each round to find the best allocation that respects constraints.

hidden.name: Which constraints are tight
paras: The hidden quantity is the set of constraints that are exactly met—saturated. If arm Red needs a 40% minimum and gets exactly 40%, its constraint is saturated. If it gets 50%, it has slack. At optimality, some constraints are tight (they drive the solution) and others have room to spare. The paper estimates which constraints will be saturated in the limit.

The paper estimates this by maintaining optimistic (best-case) and pessimistic (worst-case) upper confidence bounds on each arm's reward, then solving the linear program to find which constraints must be tight to achieve the target objective. The faster this estimate converges to the true saturated set, the fewer wasted plays occur, because the algorithm stops guessing wrong about which arms need to be played to hit their minimums and can focus plays on high-reward arms instead. Each wrong guess translates to rounds spent allocating to an unnecessary arm.

heat.caption: Darker means more impact on the optimal allocation. Boxed constraints are saturated (tight).

reads.html: At the end, the algorithm should focus most of its allocation budget on the arms and contexts that must be played to hit all minimum thresholds. The others become free to optimize.

The active set of constraints I star characterizes the optimal solution. The algorithm's convergence rate to I star governs how many rounds of suboptimal play occur before the allocation becomes near-optimal.

mechanism.h2: Why the tradeoff works the way it does
paras: The mechanism hinges on two choices: optimism or pessimism. In each round, the algorithm builds confidence bounds on each arm's reward—a best-case guess (optimistic) or a worst-case guess (pessimistic). The optimistic algorithm (OLP) solves the linear program using the best-case bounds, so it assumes high rewards are achievable and allocates greedily within the constraint. This prioritizes total reward but can violate constraints because the best-case guess was too rosy. The pessimistic algorithm (OPLP) uses worst-case bounds, so it plays it safe, over-allocating to arms with risky constraints to guarantee they hit their minima. This keeps constraints satisfied but leaves high-reward arms under-played because the pessimistic guess was too cautious.

Why does the linear program work at all? Because the problem has a special structure: the constraints are linear thresholds on cumulative reward, and the objective is total reward. The optimal solution always allocates to a subset of arms such that some constraints are exactly met (saturated) and the others are not. The algorithm does not need to enumerate all possibilities—it solves a single linear program to find that optimal active set and the allocation that saturates it.

stages.s: Observed context and reward estimates from prior rounds
Form optimistic or pessimistic confidence bounds on each arm
Solve linear program: find best allocation respecting constraints
Update estimates and check if constraints still hold

math.h2: The linear program at each step
math.words: Maximize total reward w times mu, subject to: for each arm k, the cumulative reward times w k is at least lambda k (the minimum), and all w sum to 1.
math.equation: max_w: sum_k w_k * mu_k, s.t. w_k * mu_k >= lambda_k for all k, sum_k w_k = 1, w_k >= 0
symbols: How often to play arm k (a fraction between 0 and 1)
The average reward of arm k in this context
The minimum total reward required for arm k
All arm fractions must add up to 1 (all plays accounted for)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Context: User A. Red arm has mu = 10, minimum lambda = 4. Blue arm has mu = 5, minimum lambda = 4.
Constraints: w_Red * 10 >= 4, so w_Red >= 0.4. And w_Blue * 5 >= 4, so w_Blue >= 0.8.
But w_Red + w_Blue must equal 1. Since 0.4 + 0.8 = 1.2 > 1, the constraints are infeasible in this context alone.

So the algorithm spreads plays across contexts to accumulate reward. If User B has Blue reward = 9, the algorithm can play Red in context A (even below minimum) and Blue in context B to hit both thresholds on average.
Total effect: plays in many rounds sum up; the algorithm solves the LP to find the overall mix that hits all constraints while maximizing total reward.

math.note: The linear program finds the exact mixture of arm-plays needed each round to balance reward and fairness without waste.

charts.title: Optimistic algorithm (OLP)
charts.note: Chases high reward aggressively, so it accrues reward fast. But optimistic estimates are overconfident, so some arms fall short of their minimum for a while.

charts.title: Pessimistic algorithm (OPLP)
charts.note: Plays it safe by under-estimating rewards, so every arm stays above its minimum. But conservative estimates mean wasting plays on low-reward arms to maintain the buffer.

items.html: If the sum of all arm minimums exceeds what can be satisfied (the constraints are contradictory even in hindsight), no algorithm wins. The paper handles this by showing the regret still scales well even when feasibility is barely possible.
If one arm dominates in all contexts, the algorithm must still allocate to all arms to hit their minimums. This can waste a lot of plays. The paper shows this cost as part of the regret bound.

items.b: Optimism or pessimism misaligned with true rewards.
items.html: If the confidence bounds are set too wide or too narrow, the algorithm wastes rounds learning the true rewards. The paper derives bounds assuming standard concentration inequalities hold.

By allowing aggregation across contexts, the paper avoids infeasibility in single contexts. If Red is bad for User A but good for User B, the algorithm can hit Red's minimum by playing it for User B and leaving it lower in context A.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A runnable demo simulates a recommendation system with two advertisers (arms) and two user types (contexts). Red advertiser pays 8 per show to users of type A but only 2 to users of type B. Blue advertiser pays 3 to type A but 8 to type B. Each advertiser has a minimum of 30 shows. Run the optimistic and pessimistic algorithms on 500 rounds where each round is a random user type, and plot total reward and constraint satisfaction (do both arms hit their minimums) over time.
demo.metric_eq: Regret = (optimal total reward - algorithm total reward) + 100 * (number of rounds where constraint is violated)
demo.closing: The demo must show OLP converging to higher reward but violating constraints early, while OPLP stays feasible from the start but plateaus lower. Both converge to the true optimal allocation by the end, just by different paths.
